name: Solid perception
definition: The first sign of full composition: the film organises every image around one central, privileged body. The camera oscillates between seeing as that character (point of view) and seeing that character, producing a cohesive perceiving-and-perceived subject, a 'solid I'.
deamer_quote: “all other filmic images circulate around this body” (p. 78)
deleuze_examples: Lady in the Lake (Robert Montgomery, 1947) – whole film as the detective's point-of-view shot (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Deamer (after Mitry, C1: 72) describes the 'being-with' as shot–reverse-shot couplings between a character's POV and shots looking at that character; no film named

section3.film: The Diving Bell and the Butterfly (Julian Schnabel, 2007)
scenes: Opening awakening shot from Jean-Do's eyes: blurred, flickering image framed by eyelids, blinks acting as jump-cuts and fades to black.
Bed-bound fixed POV restricted to wall and ceiling; doctors and nurses lean in too close or hover half out of frame.
His failing eye is sewn shut from the inside: needle and thread closing the frame itself.
Later he is placed in frame: wrapped in blankets on the hospital balcony, then with his children on a windswept beach, still the centre of every image.

operation: Bind the camera to one perceiver's eyes, then turn it round to look at that body, until every image in the film orbits a single subject.
shot_criteria: Either a clear point-of-view shot (framing that stands in for a person's eyes: looking down at own hands, through a vehicle windscreen, up from a bed or through binoculars/keyhole), or a single figure held dead-centre with the world arranged around them.
queries: point of view shot looking up at a hospital ceiling from a bed, nurse leaning over into frame
first person view of hands on a steering wheel through a car windshield, road ahead
view through binoculars with circular black mask, distant ship on the horizon
looking down at a person's own feet walking on a sidewalk, subjective camera
shot through a keyhole or peephole of a room beyond, dark circular vignette
close-up of a man looking straight into the camera, then reverse view of what he sees
single child standing alone in the centre of a wide empty schoolyard, symmetrical framing
cartoon character's eyes blinking open, blurry room coming into focus

name: Liquid perception
definition: The secondary sign of composition: a mobile camera and flowing montage pass from environment to environment and character to character, so centres form only for a moment before the film flows on to the next.
deamer_quote: “Liquid perception puts the camera into motion, a flowing movement of continuous reframing.” (p. 79)
deleuze_examples: L'Atalante (Jean Vigo, 1934) – the river barge and water imagery of the French prewar school (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
L'Homme du large (Marcel L'Herbier, 1920) – sea and liquid movement (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Finis Terrae (Jean Epstein, 1929) – islands, tides, rolling sea (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Deamer names the technique rather than a film: tracking shots, crane shots and Steadicams joining different spaces

scenes: Handheld long take: Lauren deflates Rose's tyre in a mansion driveway and the camera, without a cut, tilts to become Rose's gaze when she spots the flat.
The screen split into four simultaneous single-take quadrants (therapy session, lovers, a security monitor, a masseur crossing a busy boulevard) the eye flows between.
The masseur walks into an office block in one quadrant and at the same moment into the foyer seen in another.
Periodic small earthquakes shake every quadrant at once: solid ground turning liquid.

operation: Keep the camera moving and never cut: follow one person until someone else crosses the frame, then let them carry the shot onward.
shot_criteria: A visibly moving camera (tracking, crane, dolly, handheld follow) that passes between people or spaces within the shot, or a flowing water/boat-mounted movement where no single figure holds the centre.
queries: tracking shot following a pedestrian across a busy city street, crowd flowing past the camera
camera mounted on a boat gliding along a river, banks and people sliding past
crane shot rising over a crowded market square, people moving in all directions
split screen with four different scenes playing at the same time
long dolly shot along a factory assembly line past many workers
handheld camera following children running through a playground
view from a moving streetcar window, shops and people passing continuously
camera floating down a hotel corridor into a crowded lobby

name: Gaseous perception
definition: The genetic sign of perception: an acentred, non-human perception in which all images interact without hierarchy, achieved through slow and fast motion, superimposition, fragmentation, micro-shooting and manipulated film; any human figure is just one image among landscapes, animals and matter.
deamer_quote: “all images interacting with one another without hierarchy” (p. 79)
deleuze_examples: Man with a Movie Camera (Dziga Vertov, 1929) – the 'cine-eye': superimposition, split screens, speed changes (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
La Région Centrale (Michael Snow, 1971) – machine-driven camera sweeping an empty landscape (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
American experimental cinema (Stan Brakhage) – hand-worked, grainy, molecular images (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)

scenes: Slow zoom into a 3D rendering of Bruegel's Little Tower of Babel, then a black digital grid of white contour lines erupting into a similar spiral structure.
A raging sea heavily digitised; clouds racing in fast motion mirrored in a still river.
Close-up of a baby's face; the camera pulls back and up to reveal many identical babies duplicated across a white clinical surface.
Crowds in slow motion and negative; bodies seen through X-ray, brain scan and thermal imaging.

operation: Take the human out of the centre: speed up, slow down, multiply and superimpose images until the frame perceives like matter rather than a person.
shot_criteria: A visibly non-human or manipulated image: time-lapse, extreme slow motion, superimposition/multiple exposure, negative, microscopy, X-ray or thermal view, or a kaleidoscopic/duplicated pattern where no subject dominates.
queries: time-lapse clouds racing over mountains reflected in a still lake
double exposure superimposition of city traffic over a crowd of faces
microscope view of cells dividing, black and white laboratory film
x-ray film of a human skeleton moving, joints bending
rows of identical babies in hospital cribs seen from above
photographic negative of a crowd walking in slow motion
abstract animated grid lines forming a spiral, black background
stormy ocean waves in extreme slow motion, grainy film

name: Icon
definition: The first sign of the affection-image: the close-up of the face, which expresses unfilmable inner intensities either as an immobile quality (a face fixed in wonder on an object) or as a mobile power (features passing from one state to the next toward action).
deamer_quote: “The icon is a close-up of the face” (p. 82)
deleuze_examples: The Passion of Joan of Arc (Carl Th. Dreyer, 1928) – Joan's tear-streaked face in unbroken close-ups (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Broken Blossoms (D.W. Griffith, 1919) – Lillian Gish's face in close-up (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
The Blue Angel / Shanghai Express (Josef von Sternberg) – Dietrich's lit face as reflecting surface (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Persona (Ingmar Bergman, 1966) – merged faces and the face's effacement (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)

scenes: Malli in extreme close-up: large luminous eyes, lips, skin, held almost silent except for breathing and nature sounds.
Malli as hidden observer, lost in recollection, the camera staying on her eyes and mouth for a 'little eternity'.
Treating medium and full shots as close-ups: the whole film organised by the face rather than the plot of the assassination.
The ending: her face as she stands at the rally with the bomb beneath her sari, the choice never shown.

operation: Move in until the face fills the frame and hold it past the point of information, so expression becomes the event.
shot_criteria: A close-up or extreme close-up in which a single face (or eyes/mouth) fills most of the frame and carries visible emotion or intense attention.
queries: extreme close-up of a young woman's eyes, tears welling, black and white
close-up of an old man's weathered face staring off frame in wonder
child's face in close-up watching something intently, mouth open
close-up of a woman's face lit from one side against darkness, silent film
extreme close-up of a worker's sweating face in a steel mill glow
close-up of a crying baby's face
close-up of a dog's face looking up, ears alert
cartoon close-up of a character's face changing from fear to anger

name: Dividual
definition: The secondary sign of the affection-image: affect expressed by a mass – crowd, pack, multitude – where individuals are de-individualised and the group is individualised, uniting a collective reflection with each person's emotion.
deamer_quote: “The camera traverses a series of faces, captures bodies in a gathering” (p. 84)
deleuze_examples: Battleship Potemkin (Sergei Eisenstein, 1925) – Odessa steps crowd and mourners by Vakulinchuk's body (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
The Passion of Joan of Arc (Dreyer, 1928) – the judges as a gallery of faces forming one tribunal (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Strike (Eisenstein, 1925) – the massed strikers (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)

section3.film: Despicable Me / Despicable Me 2 / Minions (Coffin, Renaud, Balda, 2010–2015)
scenes: 'Minions assemble!': hundreds of identical yellow minions swarm out of labs, docks and gantries of Gru's underground base.
The horde pours into the tiered arena to hear the plan – a mass of near-identical bodies each with a small difference (one eye, two eyes, hair).
Minions working forklifts, riding winches, snacking at water coolers, doing gym class: a workforce as a single affective organism.
Minions follows three individuations (Stuart, Kevin, Bob) who carry the whole tribe's desire to find a master.

operation: Pan across a gathering until the faces merge into one feeling, then find the one face that carries the whole crowd.
shot_criteria: A crowd, pack, flock or massed group sharing one visible reaction or motion (cheering, fleeing, marching, swarming), ideally with individual faces still legible within the mass.
queries: crowd of faces in a stadium all cheering at once, pan across the stands
panicked crowd running down a wide staircase toward the camera
hundreds of factory workers streaming out of the gates at shift change
flock of sheep packed tightly moving through a narrow lane
audience of children laughing together in a dark theatre
cartoon swarm of identical little characters marching in rows
row of mourners' faces at a funeral, slow pan along the line
school of fish or swarm of bees moving as one mass

name: Any-space-whatever
definition: The genetic sign of the affection-image: an empty, disconnected or amorphous space – fog, rain, shadow, ruin, heat haze, a pure coloured or blank background – that expresses affect directly, without a face, prior to or after the human.
deamer_quote: “Any-space-whatevers utilise an empty or disconnected mise-en-scène” (p. 84)
deleuze_examples: Pickpocket (Robert Bresson, 1959) – the fragmented spaces of the Gare de Lyon (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Rain (Joris Ivens, 1929) – Amsterdam dissolved into rain and reflections (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
German Expressionism (e.g. Nosferatu, Murnau 1922) – shadow and light as intensive space (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Deamer (quoting C2: xi): 'disused warehouses, waste ground, cities in the course of demolition'

section3.film: Le quattro volte / Four Times (Michelangelo Frammartino, 2010)
scenes: A single 180-degree panning long take of a country lane: a dog patters, a truck of costumed centurions arrives, a procession forms and leaves.
The old goatherd Fuda shot small within ragged mountains and open fields, never overwhelming the landscape.
A lone tree filmed through summer, autumn, winter and spring before it is cut down.
The smoking charcoal mound: dead wood stacked and burning into inorganic carbon, filmed as pure space and duration.

operation: Empty the frame of people and hold on the space – fog, rain, ruin, glare – until the place itself becomes the feeling.
shot_criteria: A shot with no human focus (or a tiny, overwhelmed figure) where the space itself dominates: fog, rain, heat haze, lens flare, deep shadow, ruin, empty interior or blank backdrop.
queries: empty rain-soaked city street at night, reflections on wet pavement, no people
thick fog over an empty field, bare trees fading into grey
abandoned warehouse interior with broken windows and shafts of light
bombed-out ruins of city buildings, rubble, no people
heat haze shimmering over an empty desert road
smoke rising from a charcoal kiln in a forest clearing
empty railway platform at dawn under a large station roof
lens flare of sun through clouds over an empty sea

name: Symptom
definition: The first sign of the impulse-image: a character overwhelmed by a primal impulse too strong for them (hunger, sex, greed, cruelty), acting as a 'human animal' through whom the forces of an originary world pass.
deamer_quote: “how the originary world captures up a body” (p. 88)
deleuze_examples: Greed (Erich von Stroheim, 1924) – McTeague and Trina consumed by the lust for gold (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Foolish Wives (Stroheim, 1922) – predatory impulses behind aristocratic manners (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
The Servant (Joseph Losey, 1963) – master and servant in a decaying house of impulses (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Viridiana (Luis Buñuel, 1961) – the beggars' orgy (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)

scenes: Two tourists walk through a dark forest in pouring rain toward a light, reaching the stark white modernist house of Dr Heiter.
Heiter in a tailored lab coat lectures his restrained subjects on operating tables with a slide presentation before the surgery.
The joined bodies crawl on hands and knees like an animal, stripped of speech.
The camera holds too long on Jenny gagging while Lindsey reaches out to take her hand.

operation: Film a body taken over by appetite – eating, grabbing, crawling – so the act comes before any thought.
shot_criteria: A figure (human or animal) visibly seized by raw drive: devouring food, fighting, clawing, crawling on all fours, frenzied grabbing at money or prey.
queries: man greedily devouring food with his hands at a table, close shot
person crawling on hands and knees across a floor like an animal
hands frantically grabbing gold coins spilling from a sack
lion tearing at a carcass, blood on its muzzle
two men brawling in the dirt, rolling and clawing at each other
starving crowd surging to grab bread thrown from a truck
mad scientist in a white lab coat leaning over a strapped patient
cartoon character with wild eyes lunging at food
dog snarling and baring its teeth, close-up
starving man wolfing down food with his bare hands
man clawing at the dirt on his hands and knees
wild animal tearing at raw meat

name: Fetish
definition: The secondary sign of the impulse-image: a partial or special object that stores the primal force of the originary world (charm, relic, scrap, shoe), holy or evil – relic or vult – awaiting the conditions to discharge it into a body.
deamer_quote: “a special object charged with primal energies, awaiting a grounding” (p. 89)
deleuze_examples: Deleuze's list via Deamer (C1: 128): 'a haunch of meat, a raw morsel, a scrap, a woman's briefs, a shoe'
Diary of a Chambermaid (Luis Buñuel, 1964) – the old man's boot fetish (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Greed (Stroheim, 1924) – gold coins and the gilded canary cage (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)

section3.film: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows Parts 1 and 2 (David Yates, 2010–2011)
scenes: The horcruxes – Gaunt's ring, Riddle's diary, Hufflepuff's cup, Slytherin's locket, Ravenclaw's diadem – hunted and destroyed one by one.
'The Tale of the Three Brothers' in animated shadow-puppet style: Death hands over the elder wand, resurrection stone and cloak.
In the white King's Cross limbo, a foetus-like dying Voldemort curled beneath a bench – the horcrux torn from Harry.
After the final duel Harry snaps the elder wand in two.

operation: Isolate one object in close-up and light it as if it holds a power, so the frame waits for someone to touch it.
shot_criteria: An insert/close-up of a single charged object singled out and lit or held reverently: amulet, relic, idol, ring, locket, charm, shoe, key, a raw piece of meat.
queries: close-up of a hand holding a small carved wooden idol or charm
rabbit's foot good-luck charm dangling on a chain, close-up
ornate locket opened in a palm, lit against a dark background
museum relic in a glass case, spotlight, reliquary
close-up of a single woman's shoe on a floor
raw haunch of meat hanging on a hook, butcher shop
silhouette shadow puppet figures handing over a staff
stone statue of a god in a shadowy alcove with candles

name: Originary world
definition: The genetic sign of the impulse-image: a primal, archetypal background (desert, forest, swamp, the house) that rumbles beneath a determined milieu, outside history, under a curse of cyclical time tending toward entropy and ruin.
deamer_quote: “the universe tending towards disintegration, collapse and entropy” (p. 90)
deleuze_examples: Greed (Stroheim, 1924) – Death Valley desert where the final struggle happens (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Ruby Gentry (King Vidor, 1952) – the swamp as primal world (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
The Exterminating Angel (Buñuel, 1962) – the salon sealed into a primal enclosure (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Deleuze's own terms (C1: 123): 'a house', 'desert', 'forest'

scenes: A walled park with lichen-covered waterfalls and a river where the schoolgirls swim, sealed off by high stone walls.
Static camera at the mouth of a night path: Bianca passes from pool to pool of electric lamplight strung in trees until the dark swallows her.
A newly arrived girl delivered unconscious in a coffin through tunnels beneath the woods and unlocked in the communal room.
A drowned runaway's coffin burned on a pyre at night as all the girls look on.

operation: Frame the forest, desert or old house as something older than the story, and let it swallow the figures who cross it.
shot_criteria: A primal environment dominating the frame with menace or timelessness – dense dark forest, desert, swamp, cave/tunnel, isolated old house, fire at night – with humans small or absent.
queries: path through a dark forest at night lit by a string of hanging lamps
vast salt flat desert with a lone figure collapsing under the sun
swamp with dead trees and mist rising from black water
old isolated farmhouse on a hill under storm clouds
damp stone tunnel receding into darkness, lamp light
bonfire burning in a clearing at night with silhouettes watching
girls in white dresses walking through tall trees in a walled park
jungle vines and giant roots swallowing ruined stone walls

name: Index of lack
definition: The first sign of the small-form action-image: the situation begins as an ellipsis, a hidden gap, which a character's actions progressively explore and then unequivocally reveal – and the reveal reorients what they do next.
deamer_quote: “the situation is an ellipsis which is unequivocally revealed” (p. 93)
deleuze_examples: A Woman of Paris (Charlie Chaplin, 1923) – a train's arrival shown only by lights passing over the waiting woman's face (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)

The Immigrant (Chaplin, 1917) – Charlie seen from behind heaving over the rail as if seasick, then straightening with a fish on his line (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Deamer (C1: 160): the situation 'deduced from the action, by immediate inference'

scenes: Opening: a middle-aged woman in city clothes wanders a vast late-summer meadow and begins to dance alone – an image explained only at the end.
Do-joon absent-mindedly follows a schoolgirl down a dark street; she hides in a deserted building and throws a rock at him.
The mother searches for the truth, investigating the crime scene and witnesses herself.
Having learned her son is guilty, she presses an acupuncture point on her own thigh to erase the memory.

operation: Withhold what is really happening and let a searcher's hands and eyes uncover it piece by piece until one image settles the question.
shot_criteria: A shot of active searching or disclosure: someone investigating (with a flashlight, magnifier, opening a door, lifting a sheet, reading a clue) or an image whose meaning is revealed within the frame.
queries: detective with a flashlight searching a dark abandoned building
hand lifting a sheet to reveal what lies underneath
woman alone dancing in a tall grass meadow, mountains behind
man seen from behind leaning over a ship's rail, shoulders heaving
lights of a passing train flickering across a woman's waiting face
magnifying glass held over footprints in mud
door slowly opened onto a dim room, figure peering in
investigators examining evidence laid out on a table under a lamp

name: Index of equivocity
definition: The secondary sign of the small-form action-image: an action discloses a determined situation that nevertheless stays double – a slight difference relates one act to two distant situations, 'this and that', an impossible choice.
deamer_quote: “The impossible choice. The world as fundamentally riven.” (p. 94)
deleuze_examples: Lubitsch comedies, e.g. Trouble in Paradise (Ernst Lubitsch, 1932) – a closed door or gesture implying two different situations (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
The Marriage Circle (Lubitsch, 1924) – misread gestures between two couples (cited by Deleuze in Cinema 1; Deamer's Section II names no films for this sign)
Deamer (C1: 161): 'made to hesitate by a whole world of details'

scenes: Deputy Lou Ford in a sunlit West Texas boom-town bedroom: the slap, the belt whipping, then the turn from rage to sex with Joyce.
Lou slowly pulling on black leather gloves while telling Joyce she will die; she laughs, thinking it is a game.
Two murders filmed utterly differently: Joyce beaten at length in cold, unflinching close shots; Elmer shot dead in an instant and the gun placed in Joyce's hand.
A web of motives surfaces (childhood abuse, a step-brother's death, jealousy) so no single reason explains the killings.

operation: Stage one gesture so it points to two incompatible situations at once, and refuse to let the film choose between them.
shot_criteria: A single visibly ambiguous action or composition that reads two ways: a gesture that could be tender or violent, a split/forked path, two doors, mirror or double framing, a smile over a threat.
queries: man slowly pulling on black leather gloves, close-up of hands
couple embracing where the hug could be a struggle, tight framing
person standing at a fork in a country road, two paths diverging
hallway with two identical closed doors, figure hesitating between them
policeman in a cowboy hat smiling politely at a doorway, small town
mirror reflection showing a second view of the same person
hand hovering between two telephones or two buttons
silhouetted figures behind a frosted glass door, gestures unclear
